doc.title: Dan Barrett interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Internalizing time: Armstrong, Bechet and Parker
summary: Barrett explains keeping a clock in your head and how great players like Armstrong and Bechet controlled the beat, with festival pickup bands as the hard case.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: There is a concept behind that, could you elaborate on that a little bit, that is the whole concept of as a jazz musician, having to internalize time.

Yes, well it’s like a clock. You have to keep it going regardless of what’s going on around you and the best — the jazz musicians that I idolize and time recognizes, or the passage of time recognizes these people as being the best jazz musicians, and I’m thinking of Louis Armstrong and Charlie Parker, Lester Young and of course the great drummers, Jo Jones and Sid Catlett and Philly Joe Jones and John Coltrane, I don’t know, but they all, oh and Sidney Bechet, I was just listening to Sidney Bechet. He had a very strong sense of time. And he could, like the best New Orleans players, one of which is sitting across the room from us, Wendell Brunious, Bechet could play with the time as did Louis, as did Parker, as did all the great jazz musicians, where it wasn’t just playing behind the beat or on the beat, or in front of the beat, they had complete control of the beat. And some phrases would come out ahead, some phrases would come out behind, but they were all exactly where they wanted to put them. It’s kind of remarkable, even in the 20s, Bechet was probably closest to Louis I think as far as that goes. There are some breaks, I think it’s “Cake Walking Babies From Home,” one of the old recordings, where the rhythm section stops and there are breaks, and Louis takes the initial breaks and then Bechet comes in later, and it’s just astonishing what he was doing with the time, even that early. How grounded his sense of time was. So, you know, I don’t know if I’ve adequately described internalizing time, but you just have to keep that clock going, regardless of what you hear around you you know. And sometimes, especially at festivals like this, it’s almost impossible what they ask musicians to do. To get up on the stage, having never played with each other before you know, and to try and have some semblance of a beat there. To try and get four guys who have never even played before, or never even met, thinking and feeling the time the same way. You know it’s nearly an impossible task and it’s remarkable it comes out as well as it does. But sometimes things get a little shifty back there and you just have to keep that clock going in your head.
